Title: Anterior mediastinal nodular lesion segmentation from chest computed tomography imaging using UNet based neural network with attention mechanisms
Abstract: Automated detection of anterior mediastinal nodular lesions (AMLs) has significance for clinical usage as it is challenging for radiologists to accurately identify AMLs from chest computed tomography (CT) imaging due to various factors, including poor resolution, variations in intensity and the similarity of the AMLs to other tissues. To assist radiologists in AML detection from chest CT imaging, a UNet-based computer-aided detection (CADe) system is proposed to segment AMLs from slice images of the chest CT scans. The proposed network adopts a modified UNet architecture. To guide the proposed network to selectively focus on AMLs and potentially disregard others in the image, different attention mechanisms are utilized in the proposed network, including the self-attention mechanism and the convolutional block attention module (CBAM). The proposed network was trained and evaluated on 180 chest CT scans which consist of 180 AMLs. 90 AMLs were identified as thymic cysts, and 90 AMLs were diagnosed as thymoma. The proposed network achieved an average dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.23 with 5-fold cross-validation, for which the mean Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity and specificity were 90.29, 93.98 and 95.68 respectively. Our method demonstrated an improved segmentation performance over state-of-the-art segmentation networks, including UNet, ResUNet, TransUNet and UNet++. The proposed network employing attention mechanisms exhibited a promising result for segmenting AMLs from chest CT imaging and could be used to automate the AML detection process for achieving improved diagnostic reliability.

gold.abstract: To automatically detect Anterior Mediastinum Lesions (AMLs) in the Anterior Mediastinum (AM), the primary requirement will be an automatic segmentation model specifically designed for the AM. The prevalence of AML is extremely low, making it challenging to conduct screening research similar to lung cancer screening. Retrospectively reviewing chest CT scans over a specific period to investigate the prevalence of AML requires substantial time. Therefore, developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model to find location of AM helps radiologist to enhance their ability to manage workloads and improve diagnostic accuracy for AMLs. In this paper, we introduce a U-shaped structure network to segment AM. Two attention mechanisms were used for maintaining long-range dependencies and localization. In order to have the potential of Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and a lightweight network, we designed a parallel MHSA named Wide-MHSA (W-MHSA). Maintaining long-range dependencies is crucial for segmentation when we upsample feature maps. Therefore, we designed a Dilated Depth-Wise Parallel Path connection (DDWPP) for this purpose. In order to design a lightweight architecture, we introduced an expanding convolution block and combine it with the proposed W-MHSA for feature extraction in the encoder part of the proposed U-shaped network. The proposed network was trained on 2775 AM cases, which obtained an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 87.83%, mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 79.16%, and Sensitivity of 89.60%. Our proposed architecture exhibited superior segmentation performance compared to the most advanced segmentation networks, such as Trans Unet, Attention Unet, Res Unet, and Res Unet++.

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper-c contributes a validated lung-cancer screening guideline: annual low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) for asymptomatic adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-year smoking history, including former smokers regardless of quit duration. It provides an operational risk-stratification rule and emphasizes shared decision-making.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
The screening-eligibility rule (age + pack-years) can serve as a structured trigger for a smoking-cessation intervention. Because the guideline requires an annual LDCT encounter, it creates a recurring “teachable moment” where cessation counseling can be embedded. The mechanism is operational: use the guideline’s eligibility logic to identify high-risk smokers, then deliver cessation support at each screening visit.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Propose a pragmatic randomized trial in a lung-cancer screening clinic. Patients meeting paper-c eligibility are randomized to (1) standard screening plus brief advice, or (2) screening plus a cessation program timed to LDCT results. Primary outcome: biochemically verified 7-day point-prevalence abstinence at 12 months. Secondary outcomes: adherence to annual screening, quit attempts, and stage of change. Measurement uses self-report plus salivary cotinine. Validation includes comparing quit rates between arms and assessing whether the LDCT result (positive vs. negative) moderates cessation.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Lung-cancer screening identifies high-risk smokers but does not directly reduce smoking. This proposal tests whether embedding a cessation intervention within the annual LDCT visit—using paper-c’s eligibility criteria as the entry point—increases abstinence. A randomized trial will compare cessation outcomes among eligible smokers receiving standard care versus an integrated cessation program. The contribution is a scalable, guideline-aligned pathway that links early detection with primary prevention.

FINAL IDEA: Use the American Cancer Society’s lung-cancer screening eligibility rule as a recurring clinical trigger for a cessation intervention delivered at annual LDCT visits, testing whether this integration increases smoking abstinence among high-risk adults.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper-c contributes a validated lung-cancer screening guideline: annual low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) for asymptomatic adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-year smoking history, including former smokers regardless of quit duration. It provides an operational risk-stratification rule and emphasizes shared decision-making.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
The screening-eligibility rule (age + pack-years) can serve as a structured trigger for a smoking-cessation intervention. Because the guideline requires an annual LDCT encounter, it creates a recurring “teachable moment” where cessation counseling can be embedded. The mechanism is operational: use the guideline’s eligibility logic to identify high-risk smokers, then deliver cessation support at each screening visit.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Propose a pragmatic randomized trial in a lung-cancer screening clinic. Patients meeting paper-c eligibility are randomized to (1) standard screening plus brief advice, or (2) screening plus a cessation program timed to LDCT results. Primary outcome: biochemically verified 7-day point-prevalence abstinence at 12 months. Secondary outcomes: adherence to annual screening, quit attempts, and stage of change. Measurement uses self-report plus salivary cotinine. Validation includes comparing quit rates between arms and assessing whether the LDCT result (positive vs. negative) moderates cessation.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Lung-cancer screening identifies high-risk smokers but does not directly reduce smoking. This proposal tests whether embedding a cessation intervention within the annual LDCT visit—using paper-c’s eligibility criteria as the entry point—increases abstinence. A randomized trial will compare cessation outcomes among eligible smokers receiving standard care versus an integrated cessation program. The contribution is a scalable, guideline-aligned pathway that links early detection with primary prevention.

FINAL IDEA: Use the American Cancer Society’s lung-cancer screening eligibility rule as a recurring clinical trigger for a cessation intervention delivered at annual LDCT visits, testing whether this integration increases smoking abstinence among high-risk adults.

**INTEGRATION MECHANISM**  
The biomarker from Paper A is treated as a latent physiological state variable inside Paper B’s population model. Stress exposure (from Paper B) alters the biomarker distribution (from Paper A), which then modulates individual survival or reproduction—creating a mechanistic bridge from molecular response to population resilience.

**RESEARCH DESIGN**  
- *Measurement*: Replicate Paper A’s assay in two cohorts of the model organism under low vs. high environmental stress (stress protocol adapted from Paper B’s field conditions).

- *Validation*: Fit the extended model to observed cohort population trajectories; compare against a null model without biomarker mediation (AIC, out-of-sample prediction).  
- *Test*: Manipulate the biomarker pharmacologically in a third cohort and test whether population-level predictions from the coupled model match observed dynamics better than the null.

Environmental stress shapes populations through individual physiological responses, yet molecular and demographic studies remain disconnected. We propose coupling a validated molecular biomarker assay (Paper A) with a stress-driven population model (Paper B). The biomarker is embedded as a latent state governing survival, yielding a testable mechanistic model of how sub-organismal stress responses scale to population resilience. We will measure biomarker distributions under controlled stress, calibrate the coupled model, and validate predictions via pharmacological manipulation. This integration provides a causal bridge absent in either source paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: Embedding a molecular stress biomarker as a latent physiological state in a stress-driven population model creates a testable causal pathway from sub-organismal response to population resilience.
